items.title: Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS) – Qatar
items.headline: On 29 October 2026, the National International Health Regulations (IHR) Focal Point of the State of Qatar notified the World Health Organization (WHO) of two laboratory-confirmed cases of Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS).
items.body:
On 29 October 2026, the National International Health Regulations (IHR) Focal Point of the State of Qatar notified the World Health Organization (WHO) of two laboratory-confirmed cases of Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS). The cases were confirmed on 5 and 25 August 2026 and are the first MERS cases reported from Qatar since 2022.
MERS is a viral zoonotic infection, principally transmitted to humans through direct or indirect contact with infected dromedary camels. Both patients were men aged over 50 years with underlying medical conditions and occupational exposure to dromedary camels. Both were hospitalized and subsequently discharged in a stable condition.

items.title: Shamonda virus in human - France
items.headline: On 20 October 2026, the National IHR Focal Point (NFP) of France notified WHO regarding the first documented human infection with Shamonda virus (SHAV).
items.body:
On 20 October 2026, the National IHR Focal Point (NFP) of France notified WHO regarding the first documented human infection with Shamonda virus (SHAV). The case was an immunocompromised older man from eastern France with no travel history during the preceding year. He developed severe neurological illness on 23 September 2026 and was diagnosed with severe encephalitis (brain inflammation). The patient died on 8 October 2026.
SHAV is recognized primarily as an animal-associated virus, like the closely related Schmallenberg virus circulating in Europe, with no previously documented human infections.
SHAV was confirmed by metagenomic sequencing and reverse transcription polymerase chain react…

items.title: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus - Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
items.headline: Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reported eight laboratory-confirmed cases of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) infection, including one death.
items.body:
Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reported eight laboratory-confirmed cases of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) infection, including one death. Cases were detected across six locations: Al Jouf (1), Arar (1), Hafr Al-Batin (1), Riyadh (2), Tabuk (1) and Taif (2). No epidemiological links were identified between any of the cases.
All eight cases were symptomatic, most commonly presenting with fever (6/8), dyspnea (5/8), and cough (4/8). None were health and care workers. Infection was confirmed by RT-PCR testing. items.headline: On 2 October 2026, WHO became aware through media reports of the death of an employee of the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East, the Russian Federation.
items.body:
On 2 October 2026, WHO became aware through media reports of the death of an employee of the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East, the Russian Federation. According to these reports, the individual died on 2 October following hospitalization for severe pneumonia on 29 September, and pneumonic plague was suspected as the cause of death, following occupational exposure in laboratory settings.

items.title: Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus - Democratic Republic of the Congo
items.headline: On 5 October 2026, WHO was informed about a laboratory-confirmed imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) in Kenya with travel history from the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
items.body:
On 5 October 2026, WHO was informed about a laboratory-confirmed imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) in Kenya with travel history from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The patient travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to Kenya through Uganda. The patient was hospitalized and treated in Kenya but subsequently died on 5 October. Public health response measures have been initiated in Kenya and Uganda, including contact tracing.

Do not travel
to Central African Republic due to risk of unrest, crime, kidnapping, landmines, health, and terrorism.
The U.S. government has limited ability to provide emergency services to U.S. citizens in the Central African Republic.
U.S. government employees working in the Central African Republic must get special authorization to travel outside of Bangui. They are required to travel in armored vehicles in Bangui and are subject to a curfew.

items.body:
Exercise increased caution
to Solomon Islands due to risks to health, unexploded ordinance, crime and civil unrest.
Mosquito-borne diseases
Mosquito-borne diseases such as malaria and dengue fever are widespread. Medical facilities and clinics outside of Honiara are under-resourced in terms of drugs and medical equipment.
Unexploded ordinance (UXO)
Unexploded ordinance from World War II remains a significant hazard and may be present on land, in forests, and underwater locations. Many areas hav…
